The residual-based estimator, shared-component comparisons, fixed-parameter ablations, and UACQR comparisons provide useful evidence. Reported marginal coverage is generally close to nominal, and CLEAR often improves quantile loss over its individual components.
weaknesses: The conformal calibration formula is incorrect as written in Algorithm 2 and Definition G.1. With preliminary half-widths a and b, the stated score equals max((f−y)/a, (y−f)/b)−1, but its quantile is used directly as the multiplicative radius; the radius requires adding one. For f=0, a=b=1, and standard Gaussian outcomes, the written procedure asymptotically produces approximately 66% coverage instead of 95%. Lemma G.2 therefore does not hold for the specified procedure. The authors must clarify whether the experiments used a corrected implementation.

The evaluated procedure reuses the same observations for model selection, selection among approximately 4,000 mixture weights, and conformal calibration. Appendix G appropriately acknowledges that finite-sample validity is lost, but the proposed independent-calibration variant is not evaluated. Near-nominal average coverage does not establish that this reuse is harmless, particularly with small calibration sets.

Lemma 2.1 needs additional centering assumptions. Section 2.3 constructs aleatoric widths around the residual median, while Equation (3) centers the interval at the point predictor without adding that residual median. For the mean-based variant (c), skewed conditional distributions can leave a nonzero residual median even with consistent estimators. Consequently, convergence to the true conditional quantiles and the assertion that the calibration factor converges to one do not follow as stated.

The incremental contribution of dual-parameter calibration is not convincingly established. The closest matched component, ALEATORIC-R, is only about 3% worse in reported NCIW, while the fixed-parameter variants frequently match or outperform full CLEAR in Tables 8–10. Much of the headline improvement appears attributable to residual modeling. Paired comparisons with uncertainty estimates and matched UACQR configurations are needed to demonstrate a meaningful advantage from the additional tuning freedom.

The conditional-coverage claims exceed the evaluation. The real-data benchmark reports marginal metrics without subgroup or worst-group coverage. The multivariate simulation averages over directions and dimensions, which does not establish coverage conditional on individual inputs. Figures 2 and 5 also show undercoverage near the origin, contradicting statements that CLEAR maintains target coverage throughout the input space.

NCIW recalibrates intervals using test labels, making it a diagnostic of interval shape rather than the width achievable by the deployed calibration procedure. Although unadjusted metrics are provided, the headline width claims should distinguish these quantities. Additionally, Figure 3 reports baseline increases relative to CLEAR; these percentages are not equivalent to CLEAR's percentage reductions relative to the baselines, as suggested by the abstract.

Some numerical results are internally inconsistent. For energy efficiency, UACQR-P has infinite quantile loss in Table 18 but a finite interval score of 6.214 in Table 20. Under the stated definitions, these scores are proportional up to normalization and cannot disagree on finiteness for the same predictions. This requires reconciliation before the comparative evidence can be considered reliable.

In Table 15, fixed λ=1 matches or improves CLEAR’s NCIW on 13 of 17 datasets at the reported precision, while Table 16 shows nearly identical interval scores on many datasets. Figure 3 reports only a 3% NCIW advantage over ALEATORIC-R, substantially smaller than the headline comparisons. The added value of adaptive weighting needs stronger isolation and statistical support.

Coverage claims exceed the evidence. The default procedure reuses observations for selecting λ and calibrating coverage, forfeiting the usual finite-sample conformal guarantee, as Appendix B acknowledges. Appendix G usefully evaluates independent calibration, but real-data results remain primarily marginal. Lower average quantile loss and a limited family of synthetic experiments do not establish broad conditional-coverage or distribution-shift robustness.

NCIW rescales intervals using test labels, making it an oracle calibration diagnostic rather than the interval width available at deployment. Although ordinary width and coverage are also reported, the headline interpretation is too strong. The assertion that test recalibration is approximately negligible is questionable: PCS on computer changes from NIW 18.269 to NCIW 0.112 in Tables 13 and 15.

The neural comparison uses ensemble disagreement as the DE uncertainty component. It does not establish superiority over conventional deep-ensemble predictive intervals that already combine model uncertainty and estimated observation noise. That comparison is particularly relevant to the paper’s positioning against existing uncertainty combinations.

Some reported results are internally inconsistent. UACQR-P on energy efficiency has infinite quantile loss in Table 43 but a finite interval score of 6.214 in Table 45. These metrics are proportional for the same intervals under the stated definitions. The aggregation or implementation discrepancy needs resolution before the comparison can be trusted.

strengths: CLEAR is a simple, modular calibration approach with low additional computational cost. Selecting the uncertainty mixture using quantile loss is well motivated.
The empirical study is substantial: 17 datasets, repeated splits, multiple model variants, neural estimators, UACQR comparisons, and separate-calibration experiments.
Residual-based quantile estimation and combining complementary uncertainty estimates produce promising improvements over individually calibrated components.
weaknesses: The conformal procedure contains a substantive formula error. Definition B.1 and Algorithm 2 use scores equal to normalized residuals minus one, but apply their quantile directly as the width multiplier. The multiplier should include an additional one. A perfectly calibrated symmetric base interval would otherwise collapse asymptotically. Consequently, Lemma B.2 is false for the procedure as written; the implementation and reported results need reconciliation.

Lemma 2.1 does not adequately justify why having at least k consistent base models makes the selected ensemble's tail widths vanish. Additional assumptions concerning model selection and ensemble consistency are needed for the proof.

The central novelty—learning both calibration parameters—has limited demonstrated benefit over simpler combinations. Tables 14–16 show frequent near ties or losses against fixed-parameter variants. The reported NCIW gain over the stronger ALEATORIC-R baseline is only about 3%, substantially smaller than the headline comparisons.

The conditional-coverage claims exceed the evidence. Real-data evaluation primarily measures marginal coverage and aggregate losses; lower quantile loss does not establish reliable coverage for individual regions or subgroups. NCIW additionally recalibrates using test labels, so its improvements should be distinguished from deployable interval-width gains.

The neural DE baseline in Appendix D.3.1 uses ensemble prediction spread without the original DE method's aleatoric variance output. Comparison against a full calibrated DE predictive distribution is needed to support the broader superiority claims.

Reported metrics contain an unresolved inconsistency: UACQR-P on energy efficiency has infinite quantile loss in Table 43 but finite interval score in Table 45. These metrics are proportional for the same intervals under the stated definitions, so both results cannot describe the same evaluation.

strengths: CLEAR addresses a practical problem with a simple, modular approach: jointly scaling aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates. The additional calibration cost is small once the component models are trained.

The empirical study is substantial: 17 regression datasets, repeated splits, several base-model configurations, neural-network experiments, simulations, and a housing case study. The appendices provide extensive results, hyperparameters, runtimes, and ablations.

The reported improvements over individually calibrated components are promising, particularly in quantile loss. Benefits also persist in experiments with separate validation and calibration sets, providing evidence beyond the default data-reuse protocol.
weaknesses: The conformal construction is mathematically incorrect as written. In Definition B.1 and Algorithm 2, the conformity score equals the normalized residual score minus one, but its quantile is used directly as the multiplicative interval scale; the scale should include an additional one. For example, with Y uniform on [-1,1], predictor zero, and preliminary half-width 0.5, the stated procedure approaches 45% coverage at a 95% target. This invalidates Lemma B.2 as stated and contradicts Algorithm 1's coverage-based construction. Whether the experiments implement the correct procedure needs clarification.

The coverage and width claims exceed what the evaluation protocol establishes. The recommended implementation selects the mixture weight and calibrates on the same data, so standard finite-sample conformal guarantees do not apply, as Appendix B acknowledges. Furthermore, the headline NCIW metric recalibrates using test labels and therefore measures an oracle-adjusted width rather than deployed interval width. Appendix G and the ordinary test metrics mitigate these concerns, but the main conclusions should clearly distinguish empirical coverage, guaranteed coverage, and test-recalibrated efficiency.

The incremental contribution of learning both calibration parameters is weakly established. Combining the components and fitting residual quantiles provide useful gains, but the fixed-parameter variants often closely match CLEAR in Tables 14–16. Using the rounded Table 14 means, the average relative quantile-loss improvement over fixed lambda=1 is approximately 0.4%; Table 15 frequently favors that fixed variant in NCIW. The roughly 3% NCIW gap against ALEATORIC-R is also much smaller than the headline comparisons. Paired uncertainty estimates and stronger ablations are needed to substantiate the claimed robustness advantage of the additional parameter.

The baseline comparisons do not cleanly establish superiority over existing joint uncertainty methods. The DE baseline uses ensemble prediction dispersion without evaluating the original method's combined aleatoric and epistemic predictive distribution. UACQR comparisons are included, but use a different point predictor and differ in residual modeling, confounding the contribution of calibration with the underlying estimation pipeline. Comparisons using matched predictors, residual processing, and tuning budgets would be more informative.

The central conditional-coverage and extrapolation claims have limited direct support. Real-data results primarily report aggregate metrics, without subgroup or worst-group coverage. The simulations use a restricted Gaussian-noise family, and the multivariate figure averages over radii and dimensions, potentially hiding failures. Lemma 2.1 assumes consistent estimators and a vanishing epistemic component; it does not explain or guarantee the advertised finite-sample extrapolation advantage.

There are material reporting inconsistencies. For UACQR-P on energy efficiency, Table 43 reports infinite quantile loss, whereas Table 45 reports a finite interval score of 6.214. Under the stated definitions, these scores are proportional for identical intervals and observations, so both results cannot hold without an undocumented change in computation or aggregation. This requires reconciliation before the comparative evidence can be trusted.

strengths: CLEAR offers a simple, modular approach to balancing uncertainty estimates with different scales and reliability, with low additional calibration cost.
The evaluation is substantial: 17 regression datasets, repeated splits, three PCS configurations, neural estimators, synthetic experiments, and a housing case study.

The appendix includes valuable fixed-parameter ablations, separate-calibration experiments, implementation details, and runtime measurements. Reported results generally show competitive quantile loss and approximately nominal marginal coverage.
Using quantile loss to balance interval sharpness and coverage is well motivated, and the residual-based uncertainty estimator shows practical promise.
weaknesses: The conformal construction is incorrect as written. Definition B.1 and Algorithm 2 calculate scores relative to the preliminary interval endpoints, but use their quantile directly as the width multiplier; the multiplier should be one plus that quantile. For symmetric half-width a, the score is |Y-f|/a-1. An already correct interval therefore receives an asymptotic multiplier of zero. This invalidates Lemma B.2 as stated and contradicts Algorithm 1's coverage-based definition. The implementation and reported experiments need reconciliation with the corrected formula.

The default procedure selects lambda and calibrates on the same data, so it lacks the usual finite-sample conformal guarantee, as Appendix B acknowledges. Appendix G is useful, but the main text's language about rigorously maintaining coverage overstates what the default procedure establishes.

The incremental contribution of learning two weights is less convincing than the headline comparisons suggest. The reported NCIW advantage over ALEATORIC-R is approximately 3%, and fixed-lambda or fixed-gamma variants often have nearly identical quantile loss in Tables 14–16. These results do not clearly establish a substantial advance over simpler combinations and residual modeling.

Conditional-coverage and extrapolation claims exceed the evidence. Lemma 2.1 assumes consistent estimators and provides only an asymptotic result. Figure 2 shows local undercoverage and substantial overcoverage, while the real-data experiments lack subgroup or density-stratified coverage measurements. Lower aggregate quantile loss alone does not establish reliable conditional coverage.

Baseline comparisons do not fully isolate the proposed calibration contribution. The neural DE baseline uses ensemble dispersion rather than the standard predictive combination of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. UACQR comparisons also use different underlying predictors, and the EPICSCORE superiority discussion relies on results from another paper without establishing matched protocols.

Evaluation reporting needs correction. NCIW recalibrates using test labels and therefore measures an oracle diagnostic rather than deployed interval width; the available untouched-test NIW and coverage results deserve greater prominence. Additionally, Table 43 reports infinite UACQR-P quantile loss on energy efficiency, whereas Table 45 reports finite interval score 6.214. These losses are proportional for the same intervals, so the entries are inconsistent.
